title: Adjectives (nominative agreement)
blurb: Match adjective endings to noun gender — a small change that makes your Czech sound right.

vocab.example: Ten dům je velký. Ta zahrada je velká. To auto je velké.
Ten pokoj je malý. Ta kočka je malá. To dítě je malé.
Ten telefon je nový. Ta kniha je nová. To kolo je nové.
Ten hrad je starý. Ta budova je stará. To město je staré.
Ten park je hezký. Ta zahrada je hezká. To nádraží je hezké.
Ten nápad je dobrý. Ta káva je dobrá. To pivo je dobré.

grammarNote.title: Adjectives agree with noun gender: -ý / -á / -é
grammarNote.text: Most Czech adjectives end in -ý in their base (masculine) form — velký, nový, starý. To describe a feminine noun, swap -ý for -á: velká, nová, stará. For a neuter noun, swap it for -é: velké, nové, staré. This mirrors the ten/ta/to pattern you already learned for nouns — if a noun pairs with ta (feminine), its adjective takes -á; if it pairs with to (neuter), the adjective takes -é. A smaller group of adjectives (called "soft" adjectives, e.g. jarní — "spring-") already end in -í and don't change at all across genders, but you'll meet those later — for now, focus on the -ý/-á/-é pattern, since it covers the large majority of everyday adjectives.

check.prompt: Which ending matches a feminine noun like „kniha“?
check.explanation: Feminine nouns take the -á ending: „nová kniha“ (a new book).
check.note: This is the same -á you saw with „ta“ — feminine nouns and their adjectives share the a-sound.

check.prompt: „Velké“ is the correct form to describe the masculine noun „dům“ (house).
check.explanation: „Dům“ is masculine, so it needs „velký“, not „velké“ (which is neuter).
check.note: „Dům“ ends in a consonant, a typical masculine pattern — pair it with the -ý adjective ending.

check.explanation: Auto is neuter, so the adjective takes the -é ending: nové.
check.note: Auto is one of the clearest neuter nouns to remember, since it always pairs with „to“.

check.prompt: Adjust for feminine: „Ten hrad je starý.“ → „Ta budova je ___.“
check.explanation: Budova is feminine, so starý becomes stará.
check.note: Once you spot a noun's gender, swapping the adjective ending becomes automatic with practice.

title: Family & people
blurb: Talk about your family using possessives like můj, tvůj, jeho, and její.

vocab.example: Mám staršího bratra a mladší sestru.
To je můj bratr a to je její sestra.

grammarNote.title: Můj and tvůj change with gender — jeho and její never do
grammarNote.text: Můj (my) and tvůj (your) are like adjectives: they agree with the gender of the noun that follows. Můj becomes moje for feminine and neuter nouns — můj bratr, but moje sestra and moje dítě. Tvůj works the same way: tvůj bratr, tvoje sestra. Jeho (his) and její (her), on the other hand, never change — no matter what follows, they stay exactly as they are: jeho bratr, jeho sestra, jeho dítě; její bratr, její sestra, její dítě. If you only remember one rule from this lesson, make it this: můj/tvůj flex, jeho/její don't.

check.prompt: How do you say "my sister" in Czech?
check.explanation: Sestra is feminine, so můj becomes moje: moje sestra.
check.note: „Můj sestra“ is a very common beginner mistake — remember to switch to moje before feminine nouns.

check.prompt: „Jeho“ changes form depending on the gender of the noun it describes.
check.explanation: Jeho (his) is invariable — it stays jeho whether the noun is masculine, feminine, or neuter.
check.note: This makes jeho and její actually easier than můj/tvůj, once you know not to change them.

check.prompt: ___ bratr je vysoký. (my brother — bratr is masculine)
check.explanation: Bratr is masculine, so the unchanged form můj is correct.
check.note: No swap needed here since bratr is masculine — moje would be wrong.

check.prompt: Change to feminine: „Můj bratr je starší.“ → „___ sestra je starší.“
check.explanation: Sestra is feminine, so můj becomes moje.
check.note: Compare this to jeho/její, which wouldn't have changed at all in the same sentence.

title: Food & ordering
blurb: Order food and drinks politely with chtěl bych, prosím, and café/restaurant basics.

vocab.translation: I like the taste of it
vocab.example: To jídlo je moc dobré, chutná mi to.

grammarNote.title: Chtěl bych — the polite way to order
grammarNote.text: Saying „chci kávu“ (I want coffee) is grammatically fine but sounds blunt, almost like a demand — fine between close friends, awkward with a waiter. The polite way to order is „chtěl bych“ / „chtěla bych“ (I would like), which softens the request the same way English "would like" softens "want". The verb chtít changes form for gender here: a male speaker says chtěl bych, a female speaker says chtěla bych — bych itself stays the same either way. You'll hear and use this construction constantly: in cafés, restaurants, shops, anywhere you're politely asking for something.

check.prompt: A woman ordering coffee politely says:
check.explanation: A female speaker uses chtěla bych — the -a ending matches her own gender, not the noun's.
check.note: This gender ending is about the speaker, unlike the noun/adjective agreement from earlier lessons.

check.prompt: „Chci kávu“ is a more polite way to order than „Chtěl bych kávu“.
check.explanation: It's the reverse — chtěl/chtěla bych is the polite, softened request; chci is blunt.
check.note: When in doubt while ordering, default to chtěl/chtěla bych — it's never wrong to be more polite.

check.explanation: Účet means "the bill" — a essential word for wrapping up a restaurant visit.
check.note: Pair this with prosím, and you have a complete, polite request.

check.prompt: A male speaker orders soup more politely: „Chci polévku.“ → „___ polévku.“
check.explanation: A male speaker softens chci to chtěl bych — chtěla bych would be used by a female speaker instead.
check.note: Same pattern as the coffee example — only the speaker's own gender changes the ending, not the noun being ordered.
